text: In rigorous experimental design, what is the distinction between randomization and blinding?
choices: Randomization assigns subjects/samples to groups to prevent systematic bias; blinding keeps the analyst unaware of group assignment during analysis to prevent unconscious bias
Randomization and blinding are two names for the same practice: hiding treatment identity from the experimenter
Randomization requires a vehicle control; blinding requires an isogenic control
Randomization applies only to computational papers; blinding applies only to wet-lab experiments
explanation: Randomization prevents systematic bias in how subjects or samples are allocated to treatment groups, while blinding (ideally double-blind, or at least a blinded analysis when full double-blind is impractical) prevents the analyst's expectations from unconsciously influencing measurement or interpretation -- the two address different sources of bias at different stages. They are not the same practice, are not restricted to computational or wet-lab work specifically, and neither requires a specific control type such as vehicle or isogenic controls.
